text.en: Because the makkos replay the maamaros in reverse, makkas bechoros matches 'Bereishis', both meaning the beginning, and darkness matches 'yehi or', when the Yidden had light; the makkos made visible the ten powers of creation that no one saw.
The Rav reads 'vatashchisem' in Tehillim as the frog making the Egyptians barren, the opposite of yesod, which is the source of reproduction.

The machlokes between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya turns on numbers: a frog, being a mixture with kedushah in it, cannot start from two alone nor from one alone, so Rabbi Elazar describes one frog whistling to the many, one and many together.
Two belongs to the sitra achra, which is why the two masechtos of the most severe tumah, Ohalos and Negaim, both open with the word 'shnayim'.

The frog's croak, now the least beautiful song, is really 'Baruch shem', Yaakov Avinu's yichud, which in the future will surpass even Shema and the Tehillim of David HaMelech, since it reveals that Hashem reigned even where tumah seemed to be.

The Rav suggests that Moshe stopping the frogs at Pharaoh's request may mean that the time of the geulah had not yet come: had the makkah run its full course, the Yidden would have reached a loud 'Baruch shem', and they were not yet ready.
Tanya uses the word 'crowns' only for the powers of impurity, never for holiness, because the essence of impurity is that it sees itself as something and claims greatness.
Impurity is always nine or eleven, never a true ten, which is why the Torah counts eleven amos for the Teivah, eleven goat-hair curtains and eleven spices of the ketores.
In the list of the ketores spices the order by weight is broken so that kinnamon comes last, making it both the ninth and the eleventh, the two numbers of impurity.
'Re'us ruach' means a breaking of the ruach: pursuits not done for Hashem cut the soul's connection to Him, like snapping a wire that carries current.
The proof that every Jew is batel to Hashem in potential is that even sinners have willingly given their lives rather than serve avodah zarah, as with Fayvish the thief.
Actual mesiras nefesh is found only by Avraham Avinu, not by Yitzchak or Yaakov, and Jews inherit their readiness to die for Hashem from him.
The shape of the kuf mimics the hei of Hashem's Name, but its left leg drops below the line into tumah; its very name means a monkey, which imitates a man without being one.
The Rav reads the detailed description of Achashverosh's feast in the Megillah as a deliberate substitute for the Beis HaMikdash, every detail corresponding to something there.
Davar shebikdusha could be learned from the ten spies because even they had the Shechinah among them, being tzaddikim in their inwardness.
Chanukah and Purim are 'galus Yamim Tovim': days when melachah is permitted, when one does not rise to the higher worlds but kedusha descends to the lowest place.
The thirty-nine melachos ('lamed-tes') echo 'lot', curse, so melachah is a curse, and a day is exempt from melachah to the degree it is free of the curse.
The lion and eagle are holy in the Merkava but impure below, because gevurah, unlike chesed, becomes contaminated on its way down.
The Girgashi, who corresponds to malchus and to a clod of earth, left Eretz Yisrael without war; so domem, the lowest level, is batel and the Tanya lists no klipah in it.
Enjoyment itself is a human need, like air or food, so enjoying needed food is not a fall into klipah; only excess and the absence of l'shem shamayim tip it down.
Priyah is not removed but torn and pulled upward, which is exactly how klipas nogah is treated: not discarded, but elevated into kedushah.
The Shaagas Aryeh's halachic chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are not obligated in priyah is confirmed by Kabbalah: a body rooted in the three impure klipos cannot repair nogah.
Each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a part of the Torah, so Osniel ben Kenaz, by recovering the halachos of Kiryas Sefer, became master of the place itself.
Chevron, bought by Avraham, is the place of milah, and Shechem, bought by Yaakov and given to Yosef, is the place of priyah; this is why the Yishmaelim make the most trouble in those two places.
A gentile may bring only an olah and not a shelamim because eating as avodah means elevating nogah, which only a Jew can do.

The Rav reads the halachic terms literally: 'heter' and 'mutar' mean untied and 'asur' means tied, so a permitted thing that fell into kelipah can free itself while a forbidden thing is bound to the sitra achra.

A person's possessions are extensions of his own soul; when the work of redeeming their sparks is finished, the object is lost or broken, which the Rav connects to saying 'mazel tov' when a glass breaks, and someone else finds it to redeem the remaining sparks.

The Rav explains the growing chumros of later generations: borderline items are bound to the sitra achra by thin strings that earlier great souls could cut through their avodah and brachos, but this generation cannot.
Gehinnom is in essence a laundry: a dusty mattress is cleaned by beating, like the beating of the grave for permitted indulgence, while what has been absorbed needs hot water, like Gehinnom.

Bitul b'shishim is a small instance of the future purification that Hashem brings about when a soul deserves it; a person who mixes a forbidden drop in on purpose achieves nothing, just as the geulah cannot be taken by force.
Teshuvah from love is a private geulah: an individual can experience now, for himself, what the collective redemption will bring.

Like a bird that breaks free from a grip and flies higher than one that rises normally, the baal teshuvah escapes the sitra achra with greater force; since the sin produced that surge, it is rectified at its root and becomes a merit.
The Rav explains that the Jews could stay pure in Egypt yet fall at Shittim because Bilaam mobilized the full power of kishuf and impurity against them, aiming at the one thing Hashem hates.
Bilaam and Balak knew that the Jews' entry into Eretz Yisrael would lead toward Hashem's kingship over the whole world, which is why they fought it with such self-sacrifice.

The Rav reads the holy vessels taken to war as Torah and tefillah: the Urim is Torah, the Tzitz and the trumpets are tefillah, and the 'thousand per tribe' twice are Torah and tefillah, the powers of Moshe and Aharon.
Because Betzalel was a gilgul of a king, the people had to be asked about him as one asks about appointing a king, and the words 'Betzalel ben Uri ben Chur' equal in gematria 'melech biYerushalayim'.

According to the Chasam Sofer, since Shlomo rose late on the day of the Beis HaMikdash's inauguration because of Pharaoh's daughter, it was decreed that he return as Yirmiyahu to see the destruction of the house he built.
The halachah that a forbidden mixture is nullified in sixty is itself a glimmer of the days of Moshiach, since the impure klipos otherwise have no tikkun.
The nations' mercy is the same trait every animal has, so even their charity serves their own comfort, so that they can enjoy their meal knowing the poor man was fed.

Yaakov wept because a Jewish marriage is a bond of the soul that continues even after death, as the shared graves of the Machpelah show, and he saw a break in it when Rachel would not be buried with him.
Seven years seemed like a few days because Yaakov's labor for Rachel, like building a Sukkah, was itself part of serving Hashem, not a wait for his own desire.
The word zechus comes from zach, pure: a deed is a merit only when nothing of self-interest is mixed into it, and self-interest is the root of all evil in the world.
Because kedushah and impurity are evenly balanced, a person cannot tip the scale by himself; when he takes Hashem along, Hashem becomes the deciding weight.
Kelipas noga is like the thin brown skin of a walnut: removed alone it is inedible, but eaten together with the nut it becomes food.
The Masorah's siman 'noga' for the 64 pesukim of Parshas Kedoshim shows that the parsha is about raising kelipas noga to kedushah.
The halachah that the Bnei Keturah have milah but not periah has an inner reason: periah corresponds to kelipas noga, which a gentile cannot elevate.
A sefirah is named for transparency, like a window that lets light through, and so expresses bittul; impurity's powers are 'crowns' because each one claims to be king.
A child and an adult have the same middah of chesed; what differs is the intellect that gives birth to it, which directs the love to small or to large things.
The Kotzker Rebbe read the Targum's 'l'tzad' as two sides of a fence: one who wishes to stand at Sinai must be entirely on the other side from desire, and this is the meaning of sitra achra.
Ten is written as a one with a zero: below ten there is not yet full bitul, and at ten the many become 'one' again, the zero nullified to the one.
The four compartments of tefillin are learned specifically from foreign languages, because their task is to stand against the impure klipos and make the sitra achra submit.
The minyan is learned from the wicked meraglim precisely to show that only the good within each Jew joins with the others; their evil never combined.
The Aron took up no space in the Kodesh HaKodashim because something wholly nullified to Hashem does not 'occupy space', while the ba'al ga'avah, who does, leaves no room for Hashem.
The shape of the human face forms Hashem's name: the two eyes are two yuds and the nose a vav, twenty-six in all, and the mouth is a patach, the vowel of chochmah.
The sitra achra is sustained from the waste left after the good of food is separated, which is the 'behind' from which it receives, and its existence in this world is like the exile of the Shechinah.
The four layers of the walnut parallel the four klipos: three are thrown away, while the thin dark skin is eaten with the nut and nullified, like klipas nogah, which is subdued rather than destroyed.
The vav that appears only before 'nogah' in Yechezkel's list shows that nogah is a separate category from the three impure klipos, like the fourth peel of a nut that is eaten together with the fruit.

Following his rebbi, Reb Feivel Mendlowitz, the Rav explains that only olos are accepted from gentiles because a gentile's eating cannot be for the sake of Heaven, while the eating of shelamim is itself part of the korban.
The Jews offered nesachim from the very fruit the meraglim brought to slander the land, showing that a Jew can turn even something used for sin to good.
Avraham threw dust at the kings on erev Pesach because dust is bitul: as one nullifies chametz by treating it as dust, one nullifies the klipos by ignoring them.

Because the world was created through the Torah, the chachamim's psak shapes reality itself: the anatomy matches the Rambam because the halachah follows him, and a chacham can change nature through a chiddush where a tzaddik cannot.
Nogah is called a scale: the same permitted act tips to holiness or to the impure klipos depending on whether it is meant for the sake of Heaven.

According to the Chasam Sofer, the ox that killed is a soul that came down to be repaired and failed; the ban on eating its flesh is the second part of its punishment, for it loses the tikkun of a Jew making a brachah over it.

The Chiddushei HaRim explains that every sin is also theft from Hashem, since one uses the life and strengths given to serve Him for himself; this is why the Torah places teshuvah and vidui by the thief.

The Rav explains that the thief sold as a servant returns to the state of Klal Yisrael before the Exodus, so his release in the seventh year matches the pasuk that Shabbos is a remembrance of leaving Mitzrayim.
Shabbos is the dimensionless point, like the yud of a Yid, that sits inside the six sides of every object; it can be covered but never extinguished, like a pilot light, and it brings a Jew back.
The word 'chinam' means amnesty: the servant who has not repaid his theft is pardoned like a debtor whose IOU is torn, just as the Baal Shem Tov tore the document.
The Rav suggests that the six million correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Torah multiplied by ten, the number of completeness in kedushah, so that they represented the whole of Klal Yisrael.

The psak of the Torah governs nature itself: Reb Chaim Ozer told a man whose lung condition is treif according to the Rema but kosher according to the Beis Yosef to move to Eretz Yisrael, where the Beis Yosef is followed, and he lived.
Zimri's three names are three stages of one neshama, greatness, fall and rise, and the month of Av, Shimon's month, passes through the same three stages.
When Shelumiel fell, Pinchas took over the 'shalom' and the name of Shakai from his name, and so became Eliyahu, the angel of the bris.
The fox Rabbi Akiva saw, shual, is Shaul ben haKenaanis, since ayin and aleph interchange; it was part of his own neshama, admitted into the Kodesh HaKodashim because its tikkun was coming.
The Tannaim's words 'Akiva nichamtanu' are the gematria of Kozbi bas Tzur, the other half of Rabbi Akiva's neshama, which is why the Gemara stresses that wording and says it twice.
Galus always carries an ayin, seventy, as the Chasam Sofer reads in the agalos Yosef sent; the redemption is the ayin turning into an aleph, as in Rabbi Meir's 'kasnos or' with an aleph.
Zimri is called Shaul because he only lent himself to sin; unlike one who sells himself, he remained his own master and can reclaim his neshama.
Adam's garment of light, 'kasnos or' with an aleph, is the gematria of Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Shimon in his splendor.

Breathing is not a one-time endowment: each breath is a fresh act of 'He breathed', bringing a new life and a new shlichus for that moment, which is why avodas Hashem must change from moment to moment.

Even a non-Jewish king carries a spark of malchus Shamayim, which is how the Alter Rebbe sensed that the disguised visitor was the Czar, and why Moshe was commanded to show honor to Pharaoh as a king.

The knife cuts the challah, and not the reverse, because their roots differ: bread gives life and is soft, steel destroys life and is hard, reflecting the dominance of one middah over another in this world.
Trying to grasp Hashem with the intellect is like trying to see a symphony or hear a Rembrandt: the mind is the wrong sense, while emunah is a sixth sense that every Jew has in his subconscious.

Adam HaRishon is the 'challah' of the world, the separated and holy portion of the earth's dough, and the Friday challah-baking repairs Chava's sin, committed on a Friday, which brought death to that challah.

The generations, the land and the months form one structure like a fern, where each part repeats the whole: our era is both the 'heels' of history and its 'Adar', a time of hester panim, yet the heels are destined to become the head.

Rosh Chodesh Shevat is the 'Rosh Hashanah of the tree' in its deeper sense, the tree of life that is Torah, because on that day Moshe Rabbeinu began explaining the Torah, and a new flow of Torah comes down every year.

The Rav reads the Tanya's parable with modern science: the same chromosomes found in the brain are found in the hair and nails, so the remoteness of a soul is a difference of distance and garments, not of essence.
Cutting hair and nails before Shabbos means shedding the 'goy' within oneself, like a convert's immersion, because each Shabbos is a new creation and a step toward the day that is entirely Shabbos.

Following Reb Tzadok, the Gemara piles up Achan's sins to show that even so 'he is Yisrael': Yisrael, the last word of the Torah, is bound to Bereishis, the first, as the nails are bound to the brain.
The heels of Moshiach are the hair and nails of the calendar, the end of the nine months, which is why that time is called the birth pangs of Moshiach.

The Tanya's change from 'madreigos' to the Aramaic 'dargin' is deliberate: the lowest souls fall to the level of Targum, which equals tardeimah, the deep sleep of exile, and yet even they are bound to the root.
The name Yisrael holds the rosh, together with the largest letter, lamed, and the smallest, yud, while Yaakov holds the heel; so the word itself binds the lowest levels to the highest.
The difference between an olah and a shelamim is eating: since only a Jew can make eating itself an act for Heaven, only a Jew can bring an offering that its owner eats.
The Midrash's 'north' and 'south' are the places of slaughter: the nations, who bring olos slaughtered in the north, will be uprooted, and Klal Yisrael, who bring shelamim, will come.

Steam, water and ice show how one essence can be invisible and spiritual at the top and solid and tangible at the bottom while remaining the very same thing; so the differences between souls do not contradict their being one part of G-d.
The temperature of the mashal maps onto avodah: there are places where Nishmas is said cold like a snowball and places where it is a hot glass of coffee that wakes one up.

A soul's root in Adam HaRishon sets its strength but not its direction: a head soul that does not choose Torah becomes a professor or philosopher, and a heart soul that is not a tzaddik writes non-Jewish poetry.
Adam is read as the initials of Adam, David, Moshiach, so the last generation before Moshiach is the heel of that one great soul.

The Rav reads 'from My mizbeach you shall take him to die' not as a time condition but as the source of power: the beis din draws its authority over life and death from the mizbeach itself, the opposite of what Rashi's reasoning about iron would suggest.

Death by beis din comes 'from the mizbeach', the place from which Adam's body was formed, so it brings a quick tikkun and a fast return into a Jewish body; what seems the harshest din is the greatest chesed.

Following the Alexander Rebbe, being prevented from learning Torah does not remove free choice; since Torah is a person's best friend and source of help, being cut off from it is itself part of the decree.
Heaven follows the Jewish beis din: a halacha as Jews learn and rule it below is how it is decided above, so Torah study and Jewish courts actually move the tikkun of souls forward.

The Rav explains that before Moshiach Hashem settles the accounts of thousands of years at once, so the six million were given a fast tikkun and will soon return as new souls who merit to greet Moshiach.
Dovid HaMelech insisted on ruling himself, checking with Mefiboshes only for accuracy, because the psak of the king of all Israel, a soul from Atzilus, affects all worlds and all of Klal Yisroel.

Had the Maggid's students declared him the tzaddik of the generation, that ruling of a beis din below would have been accepted above; the same was true of Moshe Rabbeinu, whom the Jews should have wanted as their sole judge.

The Rav reads 'do not go up by steps on My altar' as addressed to one who has already risen: for him pride is like arayos, since both are called to'evah, and its placement before 'v'eileh hamishpatim' shows that this is strict din, not piety.

The six weeks of Shovavim stand against the six weekdays and the melachos of Egypt, and Mishpatim is their Shabbos; like the Hebrew servant who works six years and goes free in the seventh, a Jew goes free after the tikkun.

The flood generation, whose punishment was not yet complete, came back as the children thrown into the river, and the generation of the dispersion, who said 'let us make bricks', came back to labor with mortar and bricks in Egypt.
The rush of modern inventions is the hurry of Erev Shabbos before Moshiach: every person is sent to repair things in distant places, and the tikkunim must now be done fast.

The proof in the Haggadah is from the end of the passuk: before Pharaoh the brothers did not praise Egypt, or even say they were hungry, but said they came for their flocks; that is what it means to stay a stranger.
Mordechai was blamed for Haman's decree as the tzaddikim of Europe were blamed for the churban, though Mordechai refused to bow in order to be a kaparah for Klal Yisrael's sin with the image.
A ruling that seems false is not a failure of the Shechinah's presence in the beis din: it is how an account from an earlier gilgul is repaid.
The Rav reads 'tzadku yachdav' as 'just when taken together': across many lifetimes, as a gabbai balances aliyos over many Shabbosim.
The severe 'as if' and 'liable to death' of Chazal and the Zohar are the din for a higher soul, while the Shulchan Aruch speaks to every Jew.
When Rav told Rabbah bar bar Chanah 'this is the din', he meant that for him, beyond the letter of the law is the law itself.
The juxtaposition of the end of Yisro with 've'eleh hamishpatim' teaches that what is a level of chassidus for others becomes din for one who has reached it.
The shofar of Rosh Hashanah returns to Hashem the very breath He breathed into man: since that breath is beyond words, it is given back with a sound that has no words.
To show that every Jew, not only Adam, has the breath of Hashem, the Ba'al HaTanya brings not a verse but the blessing every Jew says each day, 'You breathed it into me'.
The mind cannot grasp G-dliness not because it is weak but because it is the wrong sense, as no ear, however strong, can hear a painting.
A Jew perceives G-dliness through his soul, not his mind, and sin is what insulates him from that soul.
The heel feels least because it is farthest from the head, the source of all feeling; so the last generation before Moshiach, the heel, hardly feels anything in Yiddishkeit.
The last word of Krias Shema corresponds to the lowest limb, and there the word emes is not written in the passage: at the bottom of the heel, truth is not seen.
The Rav reads Hashem's question to Iyov, 'where were you when I founded the earth', as asking in which part of Adam haRishon's body the person was, since all souls were in him.

Baking challah for Shabbos on Erev Shabbos repairs, on the very day of the sin, Chavah's spoiling of Adam who was the challah of the world, and through the secrets of Shabbos it puts blessing into the whole week.

The custom of cutting nails and hair on Erev Shabbos mirrors the souls of Adam's nails and hair: on the 'Erev Shabbos' of history, before Moshiach, such souls are cut off, as the Ba'al Shem Tov was told about the Frankists.
The halachic sign that hair and nails show a full nine months reveals the process of hishtalshelus: the same drop that first became the brain needs the longest change to become nails.
Yisrael are compared to the children of Kush because, as with black and white skin, the difference between souls lies only on the surface, the 'skin', while underneath they are all equal.

The Tanya, written in loshon hakodesh and careful with every word, switches to an Aramaic word for 'the end of all levels', because Targum, which equals tardemah (deep sleep) in gematria, is itself a low level.
Din is not the opposite of chesed's purpose but its condition: without limitation the recipient cannot take in the giving at all.
The names Yisrael and Yaakov mark the two ends of one rope: 'li rosh', the head, and 'ekev', the heel; and the yud of Yaakov is the point from which every letter begins.
A Jew who sins in a way that is an aveirah for his level, even without the literal act, is counted by Chazal as that sin; this is how the Rav reads 'as if he worshipped idols'.
The am ha'aretz who supports the talmid chacham is like the weekdays that provide for Shabbos: it looks as if he gives, but the blessing actually flows from the talmid chacham to him.
Even one who quarrels with a talmid chacham still draws from him, but from behind, in a hidden way mixed with the sitra achra.
In sleep the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's soul rose to receive secrets of Torah, and to keep 'shivisi Hashem lenegdi tamid' with the part left in the body he slept facing the Name on the mezuzah.

Each Jew's portion of Eretz Yisrael is his letter in the Torah and the source of his chiddushim; so Boaz, whose land it was, revealed the heter of a Moabite woman, while the other relative, with no tie to that place, had no tie to the halacha either.
The cut branches brought in for Shavuos wilt because they are cut from their root; they stand for Jewish souls in galus, and one davens that they return to their root.
Menashe, the wicked king, became the rav of all Israel for hamotzi; this was Boaz's comfort to Rus, that even the 'vinegar' from her would teach every Jew how to break bread.

The part of the loaf baked first is the part Hashem wants fixed first; malchus Beis Dovid is that part, which is why Hashem accepted Menashe's teshuvah before its time, through a tunnel past the middas hadin.
The berachah hamotzi literally 'takes out' the spark of a soul hidden in the bread, as Hashem took Israel out from under the burdens of Mitzrayim.
Of the three melachos of sorting, only winnowing is done by the wind and not by the person; Boaz winnowing on the night Rus came shows Hashem Himself refining the soul of malchus Beis Dovid.
The eleven melachos of bread correspond to eleven levels of klipah that a soul's spark must break through; only grain of Eretz Yisrael, plowed over its whole surface, goes through all eleven.
True mesiras nefesh means going without expecting a miracle: Avraham was saved in Ur Kasdim, while Haran, who went only because he expected a miracle, was burned.
Pesach was a rescue from suffering, but Chanukah was itself the product of suffering, and that is why the Rambam singles it out as beloved.
Chanukah closes the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, making it both a Yom Tov in itself and the Yom Tov of the siyum of all the mitzvos.
The 36 hours Adam enjoyed the ohr haganuz correspond to the 36 masechtos of Gemara where the light is hidden, and to the 36 candles of Chanukah.
The Jewish people grew into a nation at every stage outside its homeland, and received the Torah in the desert, to show that its existence rests on the Torah, which is above nature.
Shemen is linked to shemini, eight, and rises above all liquids, unlike yayin, which is seventy; so the hidden light appears on Chanukah through the oil.

Terumah and Tetzaveh are the seventh and eighth parshiyos of Shemos: Terumah, the sanctuary of wood and stone, is a lower teshuvah of 'seven', while Tetzaveh, where the kohen himself is the sanctuary, is the higher teshuvah of 'eight'.
Oil rises above every other liquid and can be lit, and fire reaches upward against the pull of the world; this is why oil receives the light of the eighth, and why its name, shemen, echoes shemini.

Pinchas became Eliyahu, the angel of the covenant, through mesiras nefesh that went against every creature's drive to preserve itself, and so Eliyahu, who is beyond nature, comes to each bris, which also goes against nature.

The Chanukah oil had to be found under the seal of the kohen gadol because the hidden light belonged to Moshe Rabbeinu, and it burned eight days because the light has no connection to the seven of creation.
Moshe was hidden at every stage, in his first months, in Pharaoh's house and in Midyan, because his whole essence is milah, the breaking of the boundaries nature creates.

Moshe as Noach and Shes: they were tzaddikim of the 'outer courtyard' of nature who survived when others were wiped out, while Moshe refused to remain alone and so rose to the inner, hidden light of the eighth.
The Rav ties the thirty-six candles of Chanukah to the thirty-six hours the hidden light served, so that the Chanukah lights are where that light still shines.
He reads the name Chashmonai as the letters of shemen and ches, oil and eight, the eight days of the miracle of the oil.
The letters of Yavan show its nature: a yud stretched into a vav and then into a nun, an expansion that pushes into the place of kedushah.
Korach was swallowed into the earth because, by denying havdalah, a foundation of creation, he undid what made him a created man from the earth.
Every Jew is a whole world with his own Beis HaMikdash; even if the Greeks break into it, the sealed jug of oil, the Ohr HaGanuz within him, remains.
The 'oils' that were defiled are a person's thoughts: the yetzer hara convinces him that all of them are impure, yet one sealed jug remains from which Chanukah's light can be kindled.
The Chanukah light's place at the door marks the point where a Jew leaves Hashem's private domain for the public domain of the kelipos; the hidden light is sent precisely there.
No one recognized Yosef because he was the hidden light; the brothers saw only a ruler, and even Yosef's greatness as a tzaddik stayed concealed.
Unlike Yom Kippur, when teshuvah rises up to the Kisei HaKavod, on Zos Chanukah the Kisei HaKavod comes down to the Jew in the lowest place, as it came down to Yosef.
The day of Yosef's test, the idolaters' festival, fell at the winter tekufah, around the time of Chanukah, so the light that saved him was a Chanukah light.
'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki' means that Hashem writes a commentary on the darkness, as a later scholar adds glosses to a Rishon no one understood; Chanukah is that commentary.

The eight nights of Chanukah correspond to the attributes of mercy from 'notzer' to 'venakeh', which are 'mazal', above any reckoning of merits; that is why Chanukah is for those whose merits cannot be counted and who live by emunah alone.
On the eighth day the nations' festival brings thick darkness, while for Jews the eighth light brings the hidden light in full.
What the Ba'al haTanya explains over five chapters, the Ba'al Shem Tov said in one word: one who turns away from the Torah in anything is already, in that, serving other gods.
The Rishonim's distinction that a Sanhedrin is fixed while the ruling that goes out from it is separate cannot be used for Hashem: His word never becomes separate from Him, it remains His essence.
Just as Dovid's 'I am like a desert bird' compares him to the bird only in being alone, not in feathers or beak, 'vayedaber' compares Hashem's word to speech only in its being communication.

Even a person's thought is not the first stage: it is stirred by a desire in the heart, as hunger makes the mind plan a meal, and that root is united with the person's self; Hashem's speech is united with Him in this way.

A turtle's shell is a garment that is part of the turtle itself; so too the garments of Hashem are His own essence. The Rav shows the idea in halachah: one's own hand on his head is not a covering, since it is part of him, while another person's hand is.
There are two true perspectives: from the Creator's side only His glory fills the earth, while from the side of the recipients Hashem created for them a world of imagination in which they live.
The word Adam equals forty-five, the value of the Name of Havayah filled out with alefs, so man is the throne and chariot for the holiness of the ten sefiros.

Tiferes is not a mixture of chesed and gevurah, like sugar and lemon in water, but a qualitatively new creation that appears when they meet, like the beauty of a painting or the harmony of two voices.
Netzach and hod are the two legs a person stands on: the right leg survives by fighting adversaries, the left by bending and bearing the pressure, both serving the one purpose of standing.
Each day of creation adds a string to the harp, and only when Shabbos adds the seventh can music be played; this is why zemiros are sung on Shabbos.
Each animal expresses one sefira, as the lion, whose name Aryeh equals gevurah, expresses fear, while man has no single defining trait because every part of creation contributed to him.

The seven lower sefiros are called double because they can be for good or for evil; Chabad can be used for evil but is not evil in essence, and the ten sons of Haman, written from top to bottom, are the ten sefiros of impurity.

The Rav explains the halachah that a gentile may bring only an olah, which is wholly burned, by the root of his animal soul in the three impure klipos, which cannot be used for good, while a Jew's can be raised up and so he may eat holy meat.
Thanking Hashem in one's mind in the middle of eating for the pleasure of the taste is itself a brachah.

The Rav explains chochmah as the two words 'koach mah', a raw potential, the first flash of an idea, and binah from 'binyan', building that flash into a whole structure, like a brick from which one builds a house.
Avraham, who loved and took in guests, embodies chesed, while Yitzchak, who served Hashem with fear and kept to himself, embodies gevurah, and these are the first two brachos of Shemoneh Esrei.
No single color is beautiful by itself; beauty comes from a blend, and so tiferes, a harmony of chesed and gevurah, is the trait of Yaakov, who combines Avraham and Yitzchak.
The teshuvah movement of today is like the drizzle that begins every heavy rain: before Moshiach a little teshuvah comes down, and with Moshiach a downpour.
The first commandment names the Exodus rather than creation because no one witnessed creation, while all of Israel saw the ten makkos, which displayed the same ten powers.
The makkos run backwards against the utterances: the plague of the firstborn, the 'reishis' of Egypt, corresponds to Bereishis, and darkness to 'let there be light'.
Bereishis has no 'vayomer' because it is the first beginning, before there was any speech; only after it could the other nine utterances be said.
A middah used without daas harms: a person who loves cookies and keeps taking more ends with a stomachache, because his chesed was not guided by his mind.
Because Avraham's chesed and Yitzchak's gevurah were each pure and unblended, Yishmael and Esav came from them, while Yaakov's blended tiferes produced only holy shevatim.
Netzach and hod are opposite strategies with one goal, to keep standing: hod, from hoda'ah, is yielding, like bowing at Modim or running from a danger one cannot beat.

The Rav explains that the Torah, like water poured into colored glass, takes on the color of the soul receiving it; the disputes of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel reflect their roots in din and chesed, and Avraham and Yitzchak differ in the same way.

Beis Shammai require two males because the world was first conceived with din, in which the male would be din, while Beis Hillel follow the present order in which the male represents chesed; in the future, when the world can stand with din, the halacha will follow Beis Shammai.

Bnei Yishmael remain the greatest ba'alei taavah despite their milah, against the Rambam's reason that milah weakens desire; the Rav concludes that a gentile is entirely orlah, so their milah removes nothing, and the holiness of Jews comes from a holy soul and body, not from a medical effect.
Because Eretz Yisrael, the foundation of creation, corresponds to fire, the root element, the Arabs who lost it were given oil, the world's fire and energy, as a cheap substitute.

Canaan, the kelipah opposite chesed, is named from 'submitting': in kelipah the female, din, is stronger, so Canaan subordinates chesed to din, and this is why Avraham would not take a wife for Yitzchak from them.

The angel sent to overturn Sedom needed Avraham's psak whether 'Moavi velo Moavis' holds, since Dovid HaMelech must descend from Lot; the angels' question 'where is Sarah' and the answer 'in the tent' gave him the psak, so he could not destroy Sedom until Lot was saved.

Yehoshua's spies disguised themselves as sellers of clay pots because a kli cheres has no worth in its material, only in its use, and so becomes tamei only from inside; the spies carried them as a reminder that they mattered only as Hashem's messengers.

The four letters of Hashem's Name, spelled out in full, become ten letters, so the Name is four in general and ten in detail; the Rav links this to a reshus hayachid, the domain of the One of the world, defined by four and ten.
Chochmah is the bricks and binah the building made of them, which is why binah is named for binyan; a sudden original insight is chochmah, and working it out with questions and answers is binah.
The letters of aryeh, lion, the king of fearsome creatures, equal gevurah in gematria, since gevurah is the recoil of fear.
A great scholar who can master whole masechtos and say a pilpul may still not be a ba'al daas, because daas means the responsibility to let the mind govern one's impulses.
Tiferes is not chesed and not gevurah but a new third thing born of their blend, like the effect when two people play the same niggun a few notes apart in harmony.
Hod gives existence through yielding: in a hurricane the strong tree breaks while the blade of grass survives because it bends.
Each of the ten makkos revealed one sefirah of creation, and makkas bechoros, striking the firstborn, revealed keser, the very beginning.
Even daas has a kelipah side (Amalek is called the daas of kelipah), but its root is good; only the middos are truly 'double', which is why the mochin alone are called mothers.

The forty lashes correspond to the forty levels of Hashem's Name a sinner blemished; he receives only thirty-nine because the tenth level of the yud, the innermost point that never consented to the sin, was not blemished.

The thirty-nine melachos grew out of the thirty-nine curses of Adam HaRishon, who was meant to have a constant Shabbos in Gan Eden; there is no fortieth because the innermost point was not touched by the sin.
Purim is a Yom Kippur of eating and drinking: Yom Kippur fasts to repair the eating from the Eitz HaDaas, while Purim, which is even higher, reaches the point that sin never touched.
The haftorah of Yehoash, who was saved in the Kodesh HaKodashim yet later sinned against it, is read on Shekalim to show that the Kodesh HaKodashim is not reached by sin.

The yud stands for chochmah because it is a bare point and every letter begins with it; the sudden flash of a new idea, in Torah or in science, is nearly prophecy, and binah is the work of developing it.
'Koach mah' means a power of nothingness, like Moshe's 'what are we', a humility greater than Avraham's 'dust and ashes' or David's 'a worm', since dust and a worm are still something.
The Rav identifies the ten utterances of creation with the ten sefiros and calls understanding this a key to much of what is written in Chassidic seforim.
Since time itself is a creation, the Torah's preceding the world by 'two thousand years' cannot mean years; it means the Torah is two levels above chesed, where creation begins.
Tiferes means beauty because beauty is harmony: a picture painted in one color is not beautiful, while a blend of many colors is, just as Yaakov blends Avraham's chesed with Yitzchak's gevurah.
Netzach and hod are two opposite ways of holding one's ground: one by overcoming, as a man with a stick defeats a dog, and one by bowing and yielding.
Every midah contains all the others, so the work of sefirah is not only on the main midah of each week but on each combination, such as chesed shebechesed and gevurah shebechesed.
Binah is understood as building: taking what was learned and building one thing upon another until a new chiddush emerges.

The direction of the hidden Name follows the story: in order when Esther invites the king and Haman, a sign of kindness; reversed in the final letters when Haman says 'all this is worth nothing to me', a sign of judgment beginning against him.

At the climax of the Megillah both judgment and kindness were needed, one for Haman's downfall and one for the salvation of the Jews, which is why the Gemara concludes to say both blessings after the reading.
A month's weather reflects its permutation of the Name: Nissan, its Name in order in the initial letters, is pleasant and kind, while Tammuz, its Name reversed, is the harshest month.
The world's leaders are like Purim players in costume: an honest Jew sees that even a world leader has no free choice to move a finger except for the sake of the Jewish people.
Haman's own advice as Memuchan, to remove Vashti, prepared his downfall: the Megillah's miracles are a chain of natural events that could not have lined up by chance.

The Mishnah says the Megillah 'is read' rather than 'one reads' it; when the reading falls away on Shabbos in Yerushalayim, the Rav says the Megillah reads itself, as it were by Hashem, and must be heard with spiritual ears.
The three longest units in Torah, Naso, Tehillim 119 and Bava Basra, share 176 because 176 is eight times the twenty-two letters, the number of Torah raised to the number above nature.
Wine, yayin, equals seventy and sanctifies Shabbos, the seventh day; oil, shemen, is related to shemonah and sanctifies Chanukah, whose eight days are borrowed from the days of Moshiach.
Bava Basra counts 176 daf only together with the missing first daf, because at the very source of Torah one does not try to understand and begins with faith.
Shavuos and Chanukah are 'cousins' through the number eight: both are free of a fixed date, both fall in the third month of their half-year, and both are read in Naso.
Cut-off Jews are like hair, which grows even on the dead; the Nazir, who may not cut his hair, holds them, and Moshiach will replant them as the crown on the head of Adam HaRishon.
Yaakov Avinu was not mistaken in seeing Moshiach in Shimshon; Shimshon truly could have been Moshiach, but the generation did not merit it.
The lion Shimshon tore apart alludes to the lion that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, the mazal of Av, showing that Shimshon had the makings of Moshiach.
The Rav explains the Berditchever's saying through the octave: song reaches the 'eighth' note, which returns to the first, the root, and that is the gate of teshuvah right beside it.
The Rav reads the two halves of 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' as the two signs by which the Rambam says Moshiach is known, and calls both a return like yovel and teshuvah.
The Torah read as a circle, as at the hakafos of Simchas Torah, joins the broken lamed of the last generations to the beis of Moshe; this union is Moshiach and the healing of broken hearts.
A Jew who looks like nothing is like a distant star that looks like a speck yet is far larger than the earth; Hashem knows each one by name.
Hashem's view of a Jew is above number, just as Tzion stands above the laws of mathematics: the Aron took up no space and the crowded Azarah had room for everyone.
The goyim's hatred through the galus, beginning with Hashem turning the Egyptians' hearts, was itself a protection, because it kept Jews from mixing with them.
The Rav reads the Tosfos story in light of the Tanya: since one who drank yayin nesech would not give his life, the chassid's later mesirus nefesh proves that the wine was permitted.

Through the Bnei Yissaschar's explanation of lighting Chanukah candles inside, the Rav says the public domain has entered the Jewish home, and today the internet brings every goy in the world into the living room.
Relative to Hashem every person is a 'peti' who believes without understanding, and the verse calls this simple belief the greatest wisdom.
Self-sacrifice for emunah works like the instinct of life: just as a sane person cannot jump off a roof, a Jewish soul cannot do something, such as denying Hashem, that would kill the soul.
Giving milah to a baby without kavanah answers Yishmael's claim: precisely because milah is emunah, above daas, it is fitting for an eight-day-old who has no daas.
A goy is entirely orlah from head to foot, so cutting does not make him circumcised, while a Jew's orlah is in one place only.

Just as among souls there is a Jew, in geography Eretz Yisroel is the Jew and other lands are the goyim; within it Chevron is the place of milah and Shechem, whose name equals 'periah' in gematria, the place of periah.
The custom of adding a Shabbos candle for each child expresses 'ner Hashem nishmas adam': every child born is another soul, another light.
The soul's longing to dissolve into Hashem is not a reasoned choice but a nature like a flame's, rooted in chochmah, which is above understanding.

There are two kinds of darkness: the absence of light, and a light so intense that it blinds, like staring at the sun; the plague of darkness was the second, from chochmah, which is why the blessing calls darkness 'borei', of the higher world of beriah.
Purim's light of chochmah is so lofty that it is hidden, which is why the day is bound to Esther, from concealment, and to 'yayin hameshumar', which equals Esther in gematria.

Walking about with a lowered head and an 'inferiority complex' is not humility but pride: the person wants to be something and resents that he is not. True humility, like Moshe Rabbeinu's, can belong to a king.

A merchant is called 'socher' from going around in a circle: his giving comes back to him, so the 'chesed' of the sitra achra is really self-interest, unlike the chesed of kedushah, which gives without wanting a return.

The Rav reads 'the stranger in your midst will rise above you' not only as foreign rulers in exile but as the goy inside a Jew, and connects it to a goy who keeps Shabbos, so one must remove it through teshuvah before Shabbos.
The Rav stresses that the Tanya's 'sinner of Israel' whose soul is in exile is not only a Shabbos desecrator but any upright Jew at the moment he sins.

Using the sun and its rays, the Rav resolves how a sin can both fail to reach the chochmah and drag it into exile: the essence stays whole in the brain while its spreading into the heart is blemished.
The Rav explains that some sinners are so steeped in sin that they almost lose their free choice and want to be good but must sin, yet even they are moser nefesh when emunah is at stake.
In the story of the Rayatz and the vessels, the Rav brings that he lifted each vessel a second time after doing teshuvah, reasoning that if he felt no holiness perhaps a sin had dulled his sense.

The Rav reads the difference between chametz and matzah as the difference between avodah zarah and bittul: both are the same flour and water, but chametz rises, a yesh, while matzah stays low and becomes a vehicle for holy names and lights.
The sitra achra itself cannot sin, since sin needs a physical body in this world; a Jew who sins lends it his body, and harnesses his G-dly soul like a horse to the wagon of his sin.

Even idol-worshippers call Hashem the G-d of gods and believe He delegated the world; their sin is the yesh, thinking their powers are their own, and a Jew who sins against Hashem's will is worse than them.
The gnat, the creature that only takes and gives nothing, is the extreme of the sitra achra, since holiness is defined by giving; yet the sinner is lower than it.

The difference between mesirus nefesh for avodah zarah and not for other sins lies in chochmah: only outright idol worship reaches the chochmah of the soul and rouses it, while an ordinary sin reaches close to chochmah but not into it.
A wild beast attacks a man only when it sees him as an animal; a person who keeps his tzelem Elokim is feared by the beasts.
Even a light sin is a branch of idolatry, not because of its severity but because any act against Hashem's will separates a Jew from Him just as idolatry does.
The 'folly' of sin is that a Jew who would let himself be killed rather than bow to an idol will not bear a far smaller sacrifice to avoid a sin that cuts him off just the same.
Because Hashem and the bond with Him are above time, a separation 'just for a moment' is not small: in that moment the person is fully cut off.
A mitzvah done in a moment is eternal, like matzah eaten once that remains forever, because above there is nothing that exists only now.
Selach lanu is said three times daily for bittul Torah, which the tamid once atoned for; the tefillos that replace the tamid carry that atonement.
The generation in the desert, who faced no idolatrous oppressor, still needed the mitzvah of mesirus nefesh, so that the reckoning of readiness to die could strengthen them in every mitzvah.
Sadness and laziness share one root in the heaviest element, earth, which is why a depressed person is also a slow one.
Sleeping late is a sign of sadness, a flight from life by someone who expects nothing of the new day; the same person rises early on a day he looks forward to.
The Arizal placed Tehillim 51 after Tikkun Chatzos so that the mourning over one's own inner Beis HaMikdash would lead straight into learning with the joy that follows sadness.
The four tefillos parallel the four Shabbos meals: the first two are obligations, Yaakov's third is a choice and the greatest, and Dovid HaMelech's fourth is kept only by the few.
Suffering comes from the hidden letters Yud-Heh of Hashem's name, so it is a greater kindness than revealed blessing, just as the first letters of 'mitzvah' are hidden by the at-bash exchange.
The proof that spiritual sadness during business is from the yetzer is that the yetzer otherwise wants a person to forget Hashem; it sends such sadness only to drag him into cravings.
The very fact that a bad thought comes is what gives a beinoni the chance to fulfill 'velo sasuru'; had it not come, he would not have done the mitzvah.
Being shaken by bad thoughts comes from hidden gasus haruach: the person imagines he is a tzaddik to whom such thoughts should not occur, when even the Tanya's beinoni is a lofty level.
The same mitzvah binds every Jew by its pshat, yet for a great tzaddik it reaches further: for him anger is truly like avodah zarah, and 'vachai bahem' means a spiritual life.
Korach was a very great man, and his jealousy of Moshe Rabbeinu was so subtle that for ordinary people it would be a mitzvah.
The plural 'matamim' points to two kinds of nachas: the sweet dish of tzaddikim who nullify evil, and the sharp dish, like horseradish made tasty, of beinonim who subdue it.
'Vegam rasha leyom ra'ah' is read not as the wicked being made for a day of punishment, but as a person making day out of the bad, turning darkness into light.
A person's lifelong struggle with a particular kind of thought may be the very tikkun for which his soul came down into this gilgul.
The Rav compares the angels who keep a person out of a heichal of tefillah with foreign thoughts to the cherubim and flaming sword that guard Gan Eden.
A thought is not empty: it is a complete spiritual entity, possibly a soul that needs a tikkun, and that is why a tzaddik can raise it.
The very fact that bad thoughts come exactly when a person strengthens himself in avodah shows that a real battle is under way, not that the avodah is worthless.
If a person had only one soul, a foreign thought would show that his davening is flawed; since he has two, the thought belongs to the other soul and says nothing about his davening.
The Rav ties the dismissal of foreign thoughts to 'ein od milvado': the same awareness that nothing exists besides Hashem is what lets a person treat the thoughts as nothing.
The yetzer hara is called a fly because, like a fly, it keeps coming back no matter how often it is driven away.

Reading 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem', the Rav explains that forbidden food blocks the heart, so a person who learns Torah, and should rejoice that he becomes a chariot for the Shechinah, feels nothing.
Food cooked at home with the words 'l'kavod Shabbos' carried holiness into it, as in the Kuzmir chulent whose taste of Gan Eden came from the Rebbe's beans; a chulent bought ready-made lacks this.
The light of Shabbos is felt in a person's face and in the candles, even in electric light on Chol HaMoed; only one with a dulled heart fails to notice it.
For the beinoni, the soul is like a drink poured into a person, a guest in his body; for the tzaddik it is the reverse, and the body is the stranger to whom one 'does kindness', as Hillel did.
Dovid called himself 'a worm and not a man' because a worm fulfills the purpose it was created for, while a person who does not learn and daven as he was created to do is worse than a worm.
A feeling in davening that does not last is not false for a beinoni: truth has levels, and only for a tzaddik is what fades counted as untrue.
The ger tzedek's answer, that even the smell of a Shabbos candle going out is sweeter than all worldly pleasures, is what the Rav says one should answer the yetzer hara.
Truth for a beinoni is measured by return, not permanence: an arousal that fades but comes back each time proves it was inwardly true at his level.
Because time is a creation and does not exist above, a sin of youth stands before Heaven as if done now.
Not feeling anything on Shabbos, when weekdays are fine, is a sign of Shabbos's greater holiness: at the king's court one is not forgiven what was overlooked during the week.
The yahrzeit customs reflect that a neshamah must pass through cleansing again before each yearly ascent, and the same holds for a living person rising in avodah.
Dovid's sin was always before him because at each higher moment he saw it anew and needed a fresh teshuvah.
Darkness is a real creation and there is a holy darkness of tzimtzum, which is why the Tanya compares the sitra achra's nullification specifically to darkness before physical light.
